chapter: The Footlight Club and Washington friends
title: Paul Jones, Buster McPherson and trumpeter Georgetown Brashears
summary: Local tenor Paul Jones battled visiting saxophonists, and Georgetown held his own against Roy Eldridge but refused to leave Washington.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: There was another tenor saxophone player, Paul Jones. There was Buster McPherson, an alto player -- he was a very good alto player. Paul Jones was the leading tenor player in town, and he used to battle with all the tenor saxophonists that came in town -- guys like, you know, Chu Berry and Ben Webster and all of them would come in there. In those days guys would come in looking for Paul Jones, or he'd be looking for them, or one of those kind of things. They'd have really these friendly battles. And they'd really play, you know!
Roy Eldridge...one of the more famous types of things that happened like that was with him. And a guy who had him

in Washington, who I understand had kind of come up with Rex Stewart... His name was Danny Bashears(?), and everybody called him "Georgetown." Georgetown, like James Morgan who I mentioned earlier, was a trumpet player that never left Washington, D.C. But he played as good as anybody in the country, including... I understand... I didn't hear the battle that they had, but I understand that Roy Eldridge came in town, and he and Georgetown had it, and it was 50-50 as to who was playing what. I later heard Georgetown, as a matter of fact I worked with him in later years. I was around, but I wasn't at that particular incident when it happened. But I worked with him later. And as a trumpet player, any trumpet player today would admire him, because he had all the qualities of playing... He had the technique and he had the feeling, he knew what he was doing -- the whole thing. The other thing about him, he had no desires to travel. He had many offers from Duke Ellington and Basie, Earl Hines, all of them, to travel, but he elected to just stay here. There are some guys that are like that, who aren't seeking the fame and fortune, the road... They're not seeking it or they're afraid of what might happen when they go out or something.
But all that was quite a learning experience to me in hearing these people play.
